content: The jaw refers to either of the two opposing structures located at or near the entrance to the mouth. The term jaws can also broadly describe the entire set of structures that form the vault of the mouth and facilitate its opening and closing. In arthropods, the jaws are composed of chitin and are positioned laterally in opposition. These structures may include mandibles, chelicerae, or, in a broader sense, pedipalps. Their primary function is to acquire food, transport it to the mouth, and/or initiate its processing through mastication or chewing. In most vertebrates, the jaws are either bony or cartilaginous and are vertically opposed, consisting of an upper jaw and a lower jaw. In vertebrates, the lower jaw, also known as the dentary or mandible, is the mobile component. It articulates at its posterior processes, or rami (singular: ramus), with the temporal bones of the skull on either side. When the term jaw is used in the singular, it typically refers to the lower jaw. The upper jaw, or maxilla, is relatively fixed to the skull and is composed of two bones, the maxillae, which are fused at the median line by a suture. Incomplete closure of this suture and surrounding structures can result in a malformation known as cleft palate. The maxillary bones contribute to the roof of the mouth, the floor and sides of the nasal cavity, and the floor of the orbit (eye socket). The jaws generally house the teeth or serve as the base for the attachment of a beak. The vertebrate jaw likely evolved during the Silurian period and first appeared in placoderm fish, which further diversified during the Devonian period. Jaws are thought to have originated from the pharyngeal arches that support the gills in fish. The two most anterior of these arches are believed to have developed into the jaw itself and the hyoid arch, which braces the jaw against the braincase and enhances mechanical efficiency. Although there is no direct fossil evidence to confirm this theory, it aligns with the number of pharyngeal arches observed in extant jawed vertebrates (gnathostomes), which have seven arches, compared to primitive jawless vertebrates (agnathans), which have nine. The initial selective advantage of the jaw is thought to have been related to improved respiratory efficiency rather than feeding. The jaws were utilized in the buccal pump, a mechanism still observable in modern fish and amphibians, which pumps water across the gills in fish or air into the lungs in amphibians. Over evolutionary time, the more familiar function of jaws in feeding became a significant adaptation in vertebrates. In reptiles, the mandible is composed of five bones. During the evolution of mammals, four of these bones were reduced in size and incorporated into the middle ear. In their reduced form, these bones are known as the malleus and incus, which, along with the more ancient stapes, form the ossicles. This adaptation is advantageous not only because a single-bone jaw is stronger but also because the malleus and incus enhance hearing. However, reptiles often swallow prey whole due to their different digestive pace compared to mammals. The presence of multiple jaw bones in reptiles may provide flexibility, allowing the jaws to expand around prey.
